strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: objective model selection and misspecification detection without ground truth in modern imaging with deep learning priors
Theoretically grounded methodology with elegant connection to marginal likelihood (α→0 limit) and sound data fission construction
Compatible with diverse Bayesian samplers (diffusion models, plug-and-play methods) making it widely applicable to modern imaging techniques
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple modalities (natural images, MRI) with strong OOD detection results (100% power for strong OOD cases)
Thoughtful treatment of limitations with honest discussion of failure modes, convergence issues, and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs
Good reproducibility with promised code availability and extensive implementation details in supplementary material
Two well-motivated scoring rules tailored for imaging applications with clear guidance on when each is appropriate
weaknesses: Limited theoretical characterization of approximation quality: no bounds on approximation error vs. α, unclear convergence rates for Monte Carlo approximations, and slow convergence observed empirically (Fig. 11) without theoretical explanation

Lack of principled methodology for selecting critical hyperparameter α: choice appears problem-dependent (0.1 for diffusion, 0.5 for blur kernels) with no systematic guidance, introducing implicit tuning requirement

Missing computational cost analysis: claims of efficiency are not substantiated with concrete runtime comparisons vs. nested sampling or other marginal likelihood estimators; computational complexity of posterior sampling not discussed

Embedding space selection for posterior-based scoring rule introduces additional hyperparameter with significant impact on results (LPIPS vs. DINOv2 changes MRI accuracy from 86% to 100%), but sensitivity not systematically studied
Experiments use small sample sizes (K=4-10, N=20-100) with visible slow convergence; reliability of estimates unclear for high-dimensional or complex problems
Limited baseline comparisons: Bayesian residual methods [55] may not be designed for same setting; no comparison with state-of-the-art marginal likelihood estimators
Insufficient characterization of failure modes: high-blur cases show 60% power but diagnostic rules for predicting when information is insufficient are not provided

Technical novelty is incremental: combines existing techniques (Bayesian cross-validation, data fission from vision literature) in straightforward application to imaging without significant methodological innovation

strengths: Novel combination of Bayesian cross-validation with data fission for single-measurement model selection in imaging, with sound theoretical connections to marginal likelihood and posterior predictive checks
Addresses a genuine and important problem: model evaluation without ground truth is critical for scientific imaging where multiple independent measurements are infeasible
Broad applicability to modern imaging pipelines with deep learning-based priors, multiple sampling schemes (Langevin, diffusion), and various noise models (Gaussian, Poisson)
Solid mathematical development with careful derivations, proper Monte Carlo approximations, and thorough analytical treatment of the Gaussian case including error analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple applications (deblurring, MRI) with appropriate statistical testing (Type I error, power analysis) and extensive supplementary details
Well-designed scoring rules addressing different aspects: likelihood-based for likelihood evaluation, posterior-based with embeddings for OOD detection in ill-posed problems
Honest and appropriate limitations discussion without overclaiming, acknowledging convergence issues, failure modes at extreme parameters, and embedding dependence
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons—only compares against single Bayesian residuals method (2021); no comparison with recent alternative model selection approaches, making relative merit assessment difficult

Ad-hoc and unprincipled α selection with no guidance for new applications; different experiments use different values (0.5 vs 0.25), undermining practical applicability and creating a hyperparameter tuning burden

Moderate experimental success rates (86.7% single-shot accuracy, 60% on MRI knee scans, 80% OOD detection) with meaningful failure modes (e.g., Figure 8 showing method fails for high-blur OOD detection)
Heavy dependence on embedding choice for posterior-based rule (LPIPS vs Dinov2) requiring domain expertise, with no principled guidance for embedding selection and no automated framework provided
Slow Monte Carlo convergence in Gaussian case (Figure 11) with incomplete resolution; while Appendix C argues fine convergence unnecessary, Figure 16 demonstrates cases where this matters
Insufficient computational cost analysis—claims of 'low computational cost' lack quantitative support; no detailed timing comparisons or scaling analysis provided
Limited experimental diversity focusing primarily on deblurring and MRI; broader application domains (CT, photoacoustic imaging, microscopy) would strengthen generality claims

Theoretical analysis gaps including limited bias analysis of measurement splitting versus true posterior predictive check, absence of finite-sample convergence rates, and no guidance on selecting K and N hyperparameters
Method assumes high-quality posterior sampling from p(x|y⁻); error propagation for difficult posteriors (multimodal, ill-conditioned) not thoroughly analyzed
Code availability not directly verifiable (URLs redacted in manuscript); reproducibility depends on availability of specific pre-trained diffusion models

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem—unsupervised model selection/misspecification detection in imaging without ground truth
Clever technical approach combining Bayesian cross-validation with data fission, with theoretical grounding (Proposition 1 connecting to marginal likelihood)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (deblurring, MRI) with extensive ablations, including analytical Gaussian case analysis and comparison to ProxNest
Works with modern deep learning priors (diffusion models, plug-and-play samplers) and is sampler-agnostic, important for practical deployment
Two well-motivated scoring rules (likelihood-based and posterior-based) with clear guidance on applicability
Strong reproducibility: code provided, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendices documenting additional experiments
Rigorous theoretical analysis for Gaussian case with analytical derivations (Appendix C)
weaknesses: Single-shot performance limitations: 86.7% kernel selection accuracy, 60% power for moderate OOD at high blur undermine claims about single-measurement sufficiency; few-shot improvements needed
Insufficient theoretical characterization of bias when α≠0; convergence to p(y) as α→0 is shown but practical bias/variance tradeoff needs analysis; α selection appears empirical
Heavy dependence on posterior sampling quality—method fails with degraded samples (Fig. 24, E.5), contradicting efficiency claims; no principled detection of unreliable samples
Posterior-based score Φ² requires embedding choice (LPIPS, DINO, CLIP, etc.) with large performance variations (Table 12: CLIP yields only 6.7% detection power); task-specific tuning needed
Limited novelty: data fission from recent work (Pang et al. 2021, Leiner et al. 2025), cross-validation established, scoring rules standard; main contribution is the combination
Incomplete failure analysis: Figure 19 shows OOD detection failure but limited investigation of causes; no guidance on when to trust results
Limited baseline comparisons: only Bayesian residuals (Vidal et al.) and ProxNest; missing comparisons to other unsupervised OOD detection methods for imaging
Hyperparameter selection (K, N, α) relies on trial-and-error without principled procedures; ablations show robustness but not selection guidance
Experimental scope limitations: kernel selection on only 3 images with similar kernels; OOD tested primarily on one ID distribution (FFHQ); MRI limited to brain/knee
Computational cost analysis incomplete—claims of efficiency need stronger quantitative support comparing to other approximate marginal likelihood methods

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important practical problem in computational imaging that lacks existing solutions
Sound theoretical framework with Proposition 1 elegantly connecting to marginal likelihood; rigorous mathematical formulation
Highly general methodology applicable to diverse imaging tasks and compatible with modern deep learning priors, plug-and-play samplers, and multiple noise models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple imaging modalities, misspecification types, and honest presentation of limitations and edge cases
Thorough ablation studies and supplementary materials; strong reproducibility with promised code release
Two complementary scoring rules (likelihood-based and perceptual posterior-based) provide flexible model evaluation for different scenarios
Honest limitations discussion and transparent reporting of failure cases distinguish this work from overselling results
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core components: data fission and Bayesian cross-validation are established techniques; the contribution is primarily their combination for imaging inference, which is somewhat incremental

Insufficient theoretical analysis: no finite-sample convergence rates, concentration bounds, or convergence rate analysis provided; limiting behavior as α→0 concerns marginal likelihood but practical α values (0.1-0.5) are far from this limit
Computational cost not fully justified: Table 4 shows 30+ minutes per image for DiffPIR; claimed efficiency relative to nested sampling is not quantified with direct runtime comparisons

Sensitivity to design choices requires parameter tuning: α-dependent performance (Fig. 2, 18), embedding selection dramatically affects results (Table 12: LPIPS 87% vs CLIP 6.7% power; CLIP failure inadequately explained), and threshold selection (95th percentile) is ad-hoc without principled guidance

Experimental performance varies substantially: single-shot accuracy 86.7% (Table 1), power decreases with noise (87%→60%, Table 2), complementary strengths of Φ¹ and Φ² suggest neither universally superior
Method inherits all failure modes of posterior samplers; degraded sample quality causes catastrophic failure (Fig. 24), limiting applicability in challenging settings
Limited baseline comparisons for OOD detection; only Bayesian residuals and ProxNest included; comparison with broader OOD detection literature would strengthen claims
